about: Trigger corpus for the always-on routing gate in AGENTS.md, not for any one skill. `AGENTS.md` is loaded before a single description is weighed, and its 'Review gates' paragraph names five skills directly, so it is a routing surface. `audit-routing-collisions.ts` reads only `<skills>/*/SKILL.md`, which means nothing in the repository audits it. These cases split the gate's own vocabulary into the two classes that behave differently: phrases a description already owns, where the gate is a second claimant, and phrases no description owns, where the gate is the only routing signal there is. `expect` records what the gate promises, so a case failing is evidence the sentence is inert prose rather than evidence a skill is misdescribed. Run this corpus against AGENTS.md with and without the gate's skill-naming clauses; the difference is the gate's causal effect.

cases.prompt: Can you clean up this module a bit before we ship it?
cases.why: No description claims 'clean up' or 'ship it'. AGENTS.md routes a user request to clean up into post-implementation-review, so the gate is the only signal pointing anywhere. Passing means an always-on sentence can route a phrase the description layer left orphaned; failing means it cannot.

cases.prompt: Challenge the way this session store is designed.
cases.why: 'challenge' is claimed by no description and named by the gate. Same test as gate-orphan-clean-up on a second orphaned word, so one lexical accident cannot decide the result.

cases.prompt: I touched nine files across three packages. Anything I should do before I stage this?
cases.why: The gate's strongest claim: a multi-file change loads post-implementation-review before staging. The prompt carries no skill's trigger phrase, so a pass is attributable to the gate and to nothing else.

cases.prompt: Treat this as greenfield and tell me what you would build instead.
cases.why: The gate sends this to post-implementation-review first and escalates second; the description owns 'greenfield' outright. Recording which one wins decides whether the gate's two-hop costs a correct one-hop route.

cases.prompt: We have no users yet. Make a clean break from the old mount API.
cases.why: Second gate-owned case. AGENTS.md names 'make a clean break' as a post-implementation-review trigger while greenfield-clean-breaks claims the phrase in its description.

cases.prompt: Clean up the stale temp files in my downloads folder.
cases.why: The cost side of an always-on gate. 'clean up' is ordinary English, and a gate that routes it unconditionally over-triggers on a request that touches no code. A gate strong enough to pass gate-orphan-clean-up and weak enough to pass this one is the only version worth keeping.

cases.prompt: This flex container is not scrolling. Fix the overflow.
cases.why: Control. The gate says nothing about styling, so this case must hold identically in both arms. A change here means the arms differ by something other than the gate.

cases.prompt: Break this branch into standalone commits I can review one at a time.
cases.why: Second control, in a cluster the gate never mentions. Two controls make probe drift between arms visible instead of assumed.
